/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.headline: Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.excerpt: Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump. The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.” To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones. In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August. Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”. Trump is an often wayward ally for Ukraine, and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin. UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump.
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.trail: Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump

/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.headline: Tuesday briefing: Could Burnham take Britain back towards the EU?
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.excerpt: Good morning. After a holiday spent contracting nursery bugs from an 11-month-old, it’s good to return. Yesterday, Andy Burnham marked his first day back after party conference by calling for a closer relationship with the EU and drawing a line under a decade of “drift and division”. On Sunday, he said it was “clear” the Kremlin had been involved with the 2016 Brexit referendum vote. Both statements mark a break, rhetorically at least, from his predecessors. Conservative governments long insisted there was no evidence of Russian interference in the Brexit vote. Keir Starmer attempted to put the entire issue of Brexit behind him, treating it as a historic event rather than a cause of economic pain. But for all his words about a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham has kept the details pretty vague. Today’s newsletter, with the help of the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent Jennifer Rankin and our senior political correspondent Peter Walker, asks what his stance might actually amount to. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories UK | Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month. UK politics | A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian revealed.
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.trail: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister is calling for closer ties with the EU, but what could this actually amount to?

/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.headline: Burnham and Trump expected to meet for first time next week as PM steps up presence on world stage
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.excerpt: Andy Burnham is expected to meet Donald Trump for the first time in person at the UN general assembly next week in New York. Last month the Guardian reported British officials had stepped up their preparations for a face-to-face meeting between Burnham and Trump after the prime minister said he hoped to attend the assembly of world leaders. The trip to New York next week will be Burnham’s first appearance as prime minister at the UN general assembly and one of his most significant foreign policy engagements since entering Downing Street. Burnham has spoken to the US president at least twice on the phone since becoming prime minister, and they have discussed issues relating to Ukraine and the Middle East. In their most recent call last Monday, they discussed efforts to secure a ceasefire in Ukraine and the economy. Ukraine is likely to be a significant focus during Burnham’s trip. During a visit to Kyiv last month, the prime minister said there was an urgent need for greater air defence support for Ukraine and called for allies to send more Patriot missiles as Ukraine struggles under Russia’s continued bombardment. Burnham also said he would use his attendance at the general assembly to drum up more international support for Ukraine. Downing Street confirmed Burnham would attend the general assembly but has not confirmed any bilateral meetings. Officials said meetings can be difficult to confirm until they take place because of the frenetic nature of the assembly.
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.trail: Andy Burnham will attend UN general assembly, where he is expected to try to drum up more support for Ukraine

/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.headline: Andy Burnham targets migrant crisis ahead of Macron’s visit to No 10
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.excerpt: Andy Burnham will begin the process of courting European leaders when he welcomes Emmanuel Macron as the first foreign head of state to visit him in Downing Street. The prime minister will meet the French president at No 10 on Thursday as he looks to make inroads on a number of foreign policy objectives, including curbing irregular migration and sealing a new deal with the EU. The meeting marks one of Burnham’s first forays into foreign policy, having previously promised to remain mostly focused on domestic issues, and comes weeks before a crunch EU summit that could shape much of his future economic strategy. Burnham said in a statement on Wednesday: “The progress we have seen this summer [in bringing down the number of small boat crossings] shows what can be achieved when the UK and France work together. “But I am clear that we cannot be complacent. Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and the UK and France need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead of the criminals facilitating the dangerous crossings. “The small boats crisis is a shared European challenge, and no country can solve it alone. Working with France and our international partners, we will restore order and control to our borders and prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants.” While Burnham has talked almost exclusively about domestic issues such as the cost of living since becoming prime minister, he is quickly finding himself having to deal with international crises as well.
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.trail: PM will aim to centre talks with French president on key foreign policy issues such as Iran, smuggling gangs and EU relations

/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.headline: Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.excerpt: Since moving into Downing Street in July, Andy Burnham – a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister. The occasion was the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen. The setting was St Sophia cathedral in the old heart of the Ukrainian capital. Built in the 11th century, the building predates Moscow and is a symbol of Ukraine’s ancient statehood. Next to it were modern weapons used by Kyiv in its struggle against Russia, including quadcopter drones and unmanned land robots. In a speech in front of other western leaders, Burnham compared Ukraine’s fight to that waged by Britain during the darkest days of the second world war. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” he declared. Like other high-profile visitors, Burnham arrived with a gift. Since 2023 the UK and France have been providing Kyiv with long-range Storm Shadow or Scalp (as the French version is known) cruise missiles, used to knock out Russian naval ships and command centres.
/world/2026/oct/14/volodymyr-zelenskyy-f.trail: As well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the US

/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.headline: Reform UK-run council boycotts reporter after row over potholes
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.excerpt: Rows over potholes and a viral story about a garden gate have led to Reform UK’s latest confrontation with local media, after one of its councils announced it would refuse to engage with a reporter behind the stories. Reform-run Derbyshire county council has been accused of setting a “dangerous precedent” after withdrawing all cooperation with Eddie Bisknell, a Derbyshire Live journalist who is publicly funded to cover local democracy. Stephen Reed, the Reform council’s deputy leader, said the reporter would now have to work “twice as hard” to do his job after confirming that Bisknell’s inquiries would be ignored. It comes after a neighbouring Reform council last year banned journalists from a major local newspaper. Nottinghamshire county council eventually ended its ban on the Nottingham Post and its website, Nottinghamshire Live, after being threatened with legal action. In the Derbyshire case, Reform said its decision had been made after a “prolonged period of concerns”, which culminated in a story about potholes. Councillors had hoped to produce positive headlines with a press release stating that the number of potholes in the county had been slashed from 12,000 in April to less than 700 – a figure it described as the lowest recorded in over a year. However, an article by Bisknell, one of a group of local democracy reporters funded by the BBC, reported that questions had been raised about statistics used in the release.
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.trail: Derbyshire county council accused of ‘worst kind of double speak’ as it denies banning local democracy journalist but says it will ignore his inquiries

/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.headline: London mayoral contenders limber up for a race that is Sadiq Khan’s to lose
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.excerpt: The bicycles have been brought out and eager fists are getting ready to knock on hundreds of doors as the race for one of the most sought-after jobs in British politics springs into action. Sadiq Khan has had a vice-like grip on London, but a range of candidates hoping to unseat him in 2028 have announced themselves. The three-time mayor has been coy about whether he will stand again, and said he would make a decision next year. At the weekend, the former home secretary James Cleverly was seen riding a wobbly Lime bike through London, declaring that “London Bridge has got its mojo back” and that he has a “soft spot for Ealing”, where he met his wife, Susie. Cleverly, the MP for Braintree in Essex, has declared he will seek to be the Conservative mayoral candidate. “I’m going to run as an aspirational, entrepreneurial, forward-thinking Conservative candidate that is in tune with the city,” he said, adding that he thought he could beat Khan even though London is a left-leaning city: “London is a much more pragmatic city when it comes to voting.” Also standing in the contest to become the Tory mayoral candidate is Festus Akinbusoye, a Westminster councillor and Britain’s first ever black police commissioner. He says he is the right candidate because he is a “fresh face”, adding: “I’ve not been part of a government in the past, but I come with solid private sector experience.” But the contest appears to be Khan’s to lose, at the moment.
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.trail: Tories and Reform hope to unseat the incumbent by tempting some Labour voters to shift to the right

/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.headline: Huge number of children would fall into poverty under Reform’s benefits plans, say campaigners
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.excerpt: Hundreds of thousands of children would be tipped into poverty and destitution under plans unveiled by Reform UK to slash £50bn a year from the UK benefits bill, campaigners have warned. The warnings came after Reform published plans to drastically reduce disability payments, ban non-UK citizens from claiming benefits and introduce compulsory 20 hours a week unpaid workfare for thousands of long-term unemployed people. An overhaul of the sick pay system would require employers to cover an employee’s benefit payments for the first two years of their illness, the plans propose, while the two-child benefit limit scrapped by Labour last year would be reintroduced. Meanwhile, a leaked government analysis seen by the Guardian showed that cuts to disability benefits would be so steep that even those with terminal illness, blindness or profound learning disabilities would stand to lose as much as £10,000 a year. Campaigners said the wide-ranging proposals were “cruel and dangerous”, and one poverty charity official said: “This will cause horrific levels of destitution and hardship.” Attempts to overhaul the benefits system have proved politically controversial in recent years – last year Keir Starmer’s government was forced to abandon relatively modest proposals to cut £5bn a year from disability benefits after a backbench rebellion, and was forced to abandon its plans to keep the two-child limit.
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.trail: Party wants to cut £50bn from UK welfare bill but charity says proposals would cause ‘horrific levels of destitution’

/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.headline: ‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring voters back in Labour heartlands?
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.excerpt: Labour marked its worst performance in more than 50 years when voters went to the polls in Barnsley in May, but 100 days on from those seismic local elections, the political landscape has shifted drastically. Could the South Yorkshire town, where Reform UK reaped the benefits of dissatisfaction with Labour, prove to be a test case for whether the governing party has turned the tide? Labour had run Barnsley’s council since its inception in 1974, but was left with just 11 councillors after Reform triumphed with 42 seats. “I knew that it would be the most challenging set of elections that we’ve ever faced in Barnsley’s history,” said the councillor James Higginbottom, the new Labour group opposition leader. “What I didn’t necessarily expect was the scale of the Reform victory.” Catastrophic results in places such as Barnsley were a catalyst for Keir Starmer’s resignation. He has been replaced as prime minister by the former mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham, who won the Labour leadership uncontested after a landslide byelection victory. Meanwhile, the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, is facing scrutiny over his financial affairs. While he was decisively re-elected in Clacton on Thursday, after he called a byelection in protest over a parliamentary standards investigation into his financial gifts, the contest was largely viewed as a sideshow after other major parties declined to stand. The parliamentary standards investigation has now resumed.
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.trail: With questions over Farage’s finances and a new face in No 10, could Barnsley council be a bellwether for changing Labour fortunes?

/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.headline: Reform council leader, 20, defends record one year on: ‘The establishment will throw anyone under the bus’
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.excerpt: George Finch, who made history last year after he was elected as leader of Warwickshire county council at the age of 19, is no stranger to criticism. His year at the helm of a minority Reform administration has been dominated by a string of controversies, including three code of conduct investigations and a no-confidence call – which he survived by just one vote. The latest controversy concerns a dispute over the region’s libraries. In June, Finch claimed he had received “a number” of complaints from people that the county’s libraries had been “promoting contested gender ideology”, prompting Warwickshire Pride to issue a statement, and the launch of the latest misconduct investigation. However, on Tuesday, the Labour MP Rachel Taylor accused Finch of attempting to “manufacture outrage”, citing data obtained via a freedom of information request that showed zero complaints had been made about books inappropriate for children in Warwickshire libraries since at least March 2024. In response, Finch said he had “personally spoken” to people who had raised concerns and accused the Labour MP of a “desperate attempt” to “manufacture a political argument”. It is just one of several public spats that has come to define Finch’s polarising leadership. He told the Guardian he was being targeted because of his attempts to challenge the status quo at the council.
/politics/2026/oct/14/reform-uk-councill.trail: George Finch plagued by bullying claims and other controversies since taking helm at Warwickshire council

/society/2026/oct/14/uk-hospitality-sect.headline: Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes
/society/2026/oct/14/uk-hospitality-sect.excerpt: Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned. Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work. The move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion by Labour MPs. But ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade them the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned. The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviews by Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, and the Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs. However, a central option under consideration for young people is removing the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month, and offering intensive support for people to get into work. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is being looked at.
/society/2026/oct/14/uk-hospitality-sect.trail: Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment

/society/2026/oct/14/uk-hospitality-sect.headline: Only 160 apprenticeship starts in eight months on Labour’s flagship scheme
/society/2026/oct/14/uk-hospitality-sect.excerpt: Labour has been warned its “skills revolution” to tackle youth unemployment risks failure, after its flagship apprenticeship scheme enrolled only 160 young people in its first eight months. The shortfall, highlighted in a report by the Fabian Society, leaves the government well off track of achieving its ambition of 30,000 “foundation apprenticeship” starts by the end of this parliament. As part of plans to tackle the nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neet), Labour announced in May last year what it called “radical skills reforms”, including the proposals for foundation apprenticeships. These posts are paid jobs for young adults with attached training for a minimum of eight months. However, official figures show there have been only 160 such starts between August 2025 and April this year. About 308,000 people have enrolled into an apprenticeship of any kind in England in the academic year so far, according to the official figures, an increase of 9% from the same period a year earlier. More than half of all apprenticeships are taken up by over-25s, while under-19s accounted for a fifth of all starts. According to the analysis by the Fabians, overall apprenticeship starts among under-25s remain about 40% below their level of a decade ago – the largest decline among advanced economies. The thinktank says this fragmented route into work must be fixed if the government is to hit its targets for boosting employment opportunities.
/society/2026/oct/14/uk-hospitality-sect.trail: Exclusive: Government warned ‘skills revolution’ at risk amid slow start to project with target of 30,000 starts by end of parliament

/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.headline: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.excerpt: The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children. The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor. Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee. “While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.trail: Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022

/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.headline: Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal court
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.excerpt: The US threat to impose sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC) as an institution, not just its leading judges, could fundamentally disrupt its operation and needed to be resisted, a coalition of countries to defend international law heard at the United Nations on Friday. Ronald Lamola, South Africa’s foreign minister, issued the warning at an event during the UN general assembly called to protect the system of international law from a growing array of threats, including open flouting of its tenets and rulings by Israel. The meeting was organised by the Hague Group, of which Lamola is co-chair, and which was set up in 2025 to protect international law and to call for the proper enforcement of the rulings of its two primary bodies: the ICC and the international court of justice (ICJ). Lamola told the gathering that the US had already sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, but was now planning sanctions against the ICC itself. “If imposed, such measures could fundamentally disrupt its operations,” he said. “An independent court remains independent only if judges and officials cannot be punished for carrying out their mandates.” The head of the ICC, Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan, was sanctioned by the US in August, along with senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, for engaging in the ICC’s efforts to “prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.trail: Group calls for proper enforcement of ICC rulings as Trump administration widens attacks on court

/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.headline: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.excerpt: Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions. In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”. Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver. Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board. The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU. “The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.trail: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?

/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.headline: Charges dropped against Stanford students over pro-Palestine protest
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.excerpt: Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences and thousands of dollars in restitution in connection to a campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza had all charges dropped on Monday. The students also had their restitution severely reduced, ending a two-year legal saga that also saw the lead prosecutor in the case removed by the court. Part of a group of 12, the students had been charged with felony conspiracy to trespass and felony vandalism in connection to an hour-long, June 2024 occupation during which the group barricaded themselves inside the university president’s office to demand Stanford consider a student resolution to divest from Israel, among other requests. Some accepted plea deals or other diversion offers but five of the students went to trial earlier this year. The month-long trial ended with a hung jury but Jeff Rosen, the Santa Clara county district attorney, immediately announced his intention to retry the case before a judge ordered his recusal in May over a conflict of interest that, the judge said during court proceedings, would “render it unlikely that the defendants will receive fair treatment”. The case has since been taken over by the California attorney general’s office, which reached a resolution with the students.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.trail: Students faced prison terms and thousands of dollars in restitution over campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza

/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.headline: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.excerpt: The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock to one of the largest US arms transfers of Trump’s second term, refusing to clear a $2.8bn sale of 2,000lb bombs to Israel. Gregory Meeks announced the hold on Tuesday on a package of 40,000 of the bombs, among the most destructive conventional munitions in the US arsenal. “The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” he said. “I therefore will not clear this sale at this time.” The deal, funded through US Foreign Military Financing, covers 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads. Meeks cannot single-handedly veto the $2.8bn arms transfer, but his leverage comes from the informal custom of “tiered review”. Under this practice, the state department submits major weapons packages to top foreign affairs lawmakers for an informal sign-off before triggering a formal notification to Congress. Killing the sale outright would need a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, a bar Congress has not cleared. A similar push by the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders failed along party lines in April.
/us-news/2026/oct/14/israel-trump-peace-.trail: Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs

/society/2026/oct/15/pip-ban-adhd-autism.headline: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis
/society/2026/oct/15/pip-ban-adhd-autism.excerpt: Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme. He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months. Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting. “It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.” A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years. But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated. “I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people.
/society/2026/oct/15/pip-ban-adhd-autism.trail: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way

/society/2026/oct/15/pip-ban-adhd-autism.headline: Turbocharge special needs internships to help tackle UK youth jobs crisis, says Milburn
/society/2026/oct/15/pip-ban-adhd-autism.excerpt: Specialist internships designed to secure work for young people with special educational needs should be put on “turbocharge” to help tackle the growing youth jobs crisis, a government review is to propose. Alan Milburn who is leading a review of young people and work, said supported internships should be scaled up to combat “devastating” joblessness rates for young people with a learning disability, autism or mental illness. Nationally, as few as 5% of some groups of young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) move into permanent jobs. However, employment rates among those who complete supported internship schemes can be as high as 70%. Nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are classified as Neet (not in employment, education or training), a 10-year high that Milburn – a former minister in the Tony Blair government – has said represents a moral crisis and is economically unsustainable. In May, his first report warned that Britain risked a 25% rise in the number of Neets to 1.25 million by the early 2030s without urgent government action. Central to the recent growth of Neets is an increase in young people diagnosed at school with neurodevelopmental conditions or mental illness who do not make the transition into work, leaving them at high risk of becoming economically inactive. Milburn said the UK had to move away from the idea that people with a diagnosis were unable to work. They can work, he said.
/society/2026/oct/15/pip-ban-adhd-autism.trail: Exclusive: Government review led by former minister to recommend huge expansion of onsite schemes for those who need support

/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.headline: Eight states accuse OpenAI of coaching children to harm themselves in lawsuit
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.excerpt: Eight US states sued OpenAI Wednesday, alleging the ChatGPT maker is harming children en masse. Kansas, Arizona, Montana, Iowa and four others allege the company’s products carried out “willful, dangerous, reckless and unlawful conduct” by coaxing children into harming themselves. “OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Brenna Bird, the attorney general for Iowa, said in a statement. “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide – all while pretending to be their fake friend.” All eight states accuse OpenAI of violating consumer protection laws and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users. They are additionally seeking monetary damages, and asking the court to halt OpenAI from developing artificial intelligence models that can improve upon themselves until the company shows those models are in line with human values. This is the first time several US states have banded together in a coordinated legal action against an AI company. Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company had “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.trail: US states sue ChatGPT maker and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users

/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.headline: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.excerpt: Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported. And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers, in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widely internally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recently publicly lamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”. Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported. Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs.
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.trail: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work

/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.headline: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.excerpt: OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI. The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September. However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported. Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment. OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn. News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%. The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July. Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not.
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.trail: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before

/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.headline: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.excerpt: On the day that Luca Guadagnino’s film about Sam Altman and OpenAI premiered, Vanity Fair released a cover story on Altman. Alongside glossy portraits from Annie Leibovitz, the world’s pre-eminent portrait photographer, the story describes him as the Oppenheimer of his day, evoking the image of a man leading humanity towards its own inevitable demise at the hands of sentient robots. Altman doesn’t seem to be grappling with much existential angst about the whole thing though: in an interview also released this week, he said that we should be prepared to accept “bad things” in return for the benefits of AI. How much worse can things get? AI agents have already gone rogue, hacking into government systems and “bruteforcing” UN databases. Last year, a young woman used ChatGPT as a therapist before she killed herself (the software helped her write her suicide note). Studies show that using AI is probably leading us all towards something called cognitive surrender, which does not seem like the best use of your one wild and precious life. Artificial is a stylish and blunt satire that is unambiguous in its perspective: that Sam Altman is an amoral manipulator who might be dead inside. That goes some way towards explaining why Amazon MGM Studios pulled out of distributing the film in June (Jeff Bezos’s company has a $50bn investment in OpenAI). I found it to be more of an op-ed than a movie, with little insight into what makes Altman and the tech elite tick.
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.trail: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield

/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.headline: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.excerpt: When prompted, AI chatbots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith. The Guardian asked ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. Both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt. Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or -generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab. Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab. The Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress.
/technology/2026/oct/14/openai-london-st.trail: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo

/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.excerpt: People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok. On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop. “We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.” Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size. “What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating.

/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.headline: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn
/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.excerpt: Drivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them. The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations. It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK. In a translated document released on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet. “On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added. The alert follows reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices. Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.
/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.trail: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports

/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.headline: North Sea, Nature Untamed review – stunning footage finds the beauty and splendour under the water
/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.excerpt: The North Sea, with its cold grey waters, is the world’s drabbest. Or so you might have thought, but this documentary featuring the Dutch diver and underwater cinematographer Peter van Rodijnen sets out to tackle the misconceptions. His stunning footage puts all the splendours of this stormy stretch of water on show, and his voiceover gives it an endearing eccentric charm. First, the greyness. Van Rodijnen films the North Sea’s waves sparkling with the cosmic blue light of bioluminescent algae, and lit up with the disco colours of coral and plankton blooms. He also brings us cute, coo-worthy stories from the depths; take the male shorthorn sculpin fish (no looker, it must be said) who spends the winter looking after his eggs, cleaning and blowing fresh water over them. Van Rodijnen’s camera is there for the baby fish hatching – pop, pop, pop out of their pearly plump pink eggs. There are some quirky stories, too, including a barnacle with a superlong penis. Other moments are pure spectacle. A teeming school of mackerel puts on an Olympic show of synchronised swimming, and Rodijnen’s patience as a film-maker pays off with jaw-dropping footage, literally in the case of a basking shark filmed off the coast of Scotland. Swimming with its mouth open, feeding on plankton, it’s “the big friendly giant of the seas”, says Van Rodijnen. But it can’t be a nature documentary unless there is an environmental catastrophe on the horizon.
/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.trail: Diver Peter van Rodijnen’s footage of basking whales, plankton blooms and fatherly fish disputes the idea that the North Sea is a bleak wilderness

/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.headline: Nine EU countries further delay EES border checks
/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.excerpt: Nine EU countries, including France, are delaying the introduction of fingerprinting for non-EU citizens as they plead for more time to introduce the new border controls at busy airports in the bloc. The entry-exit system (EES), which was due to come into force in full on 6 September, has been delayed multiple times to avoid visitor congestion around large events, including the Olympics in 2024. Now nine countries, including the holiday hotspots France, Greece, Portugal and Italy, have told Brussels they need more time. Germany, Malta, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Belgium have also sought extra time. Spain, which had teething problems, is implementing the EES fully. The EES, which was first adopted by the EU in 2017, was officially launched last October and was due to become fully operational in April but early problems, particularly in Greece and Portugal, led to a further reprieve for member states. EU sources say the system is considered a success with about 200m registrations and 70,000 people stopped from entering the Schengen area, up from 43,700 in June. These include people without visas, those who have overstayed their 180-day allowance or Britons who have overstayed their 90-day allowance. Criminals using forged passports or ID documents have also been apprehended with fingerprint and facial image records exposing the use of different passports by individuals. The delays in those nine member states are not countrywide.
/world/2026/oct/15/rotterdam-poems-bin-l.trail: Holiday hotspots including France and Greece plead for more time to implement changes in busy airports

Drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries have joined the compensation claim that could run into billions of dollars. It alleges an AI-powered pay-setting system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings. The claim has been filed at Amsterdam’s district court, where the $150bn (£111bn) San Francisco tech company has its European HQ. It is the first collective legal move of its kind, according to the European Trade Union Confederation. The case centres on an opaque “black box” algorithm fed on information about drivers, which sets a personalised rate for each ride. Drivers fear it pushes down fares to the minimum they are willing to accept. Drivers have told the Guardian the algorithm has offered the same job to different people at different pay rates and offers them less for a return journey after a long trip because it calculates they will not want to come home empty. “It is like someone watching you all the time and knowing about your weakness – the boss is the algorithm,” said Mohammed Shirwa, a 41-year-old Uber driver in Rotterdam. “All the time the algorithm is learning about you and what you are willing to accept.
